The following is part of the evidence before the House of Lords, given by the Hon. and Rev. B. W Noel, on the question—“As a proof of how little such a system can prevail, I find that, when the Kildare Place Society came to Parliament annually for the money which they wanted, after ten years of exertions, they only got 29,812 children in their schools out of a half a million that ought to have been instructed; and this was at a fearful sacrifice, much greater than the board is called to make, for the religious education was often merely nominal, and the Bible was not often read. The Commissioners of the Education Inquiry state that they found the reading of the Scriptures to be frequently mere form, and, in the second place, no exposition was allowed; and, not withstanding these fatal concessions, after all, in ten years, they could only get out of 500,000 Roman Catholic children, 29,812.” —Lords, p. 872.

* The ignorance of one class respecting the condition of another in this country is very remarkable. A friend of ours once heard a district of Manchester, which is chiefly occupied by the working men, described by ladies and gentlemen in that town as extremely wretched, and not even safe for a stranger to pass through. He had the courage to go and use his own eyes, when he found that the dwellings were generally comfortable, and the people to all appearance decent. He went and went again to that district, at various hours of the day, and always found every thing quiet. Notions in the same degree erroneous probably exist in every large city respecting the occupants of certain districts. Popular not on in general, are apt long to survive any basis of fact which they originally had. There is a disagreeable disease, supposed by the lower order in England to be particularly prevalent in Scotland: what prevalence it may have had ages ago we cannot tell; but it is a curious fact that, though we have spent all the years of our life in Scotland, we never once saw a person known to be afflicted with that disease.
